first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent this because the groom's family is Nigerian and I honestly didn't know where to begin. The opening tells me straight away that the families do a great deal of it, which is me. It's calm, there's no silly slang, and the paragraphs are short enough on the iPad. Lots of new words, but I kept going.

journey.quote: Two families meet, ask, answer, present gifts and settle a list, and only then does the public celebration arrive, with its matching fabric, its music and a dance floor that fills fast.
journey.reaction: So the parents are in it from the very start. Good to know before I'm sitting in someone's lounge room wondering what's expected of me.

journey.quote: Smartraveller advises Australians to reconsider travel to Nigeria, so many diaspora couples bring these customs to a wedding in Australia or at another destination.
journey.reaction: Thank you for being upfront. That's the first thing my husband would have looked up, and it's right there at the top.

journey.section: Nigerian wedding ceremony traditions, in two parts
journey.quote: The faith or civil ceremony, a church wedding, a nikah or a registry, often falls on another day.
journey.reaction: Two weddings. Well. That's two venues, two lots of catering and possibly two trips for Nana. I'd need to sit down with the other family about this early.

journey.section: 1. The introduction and the engagement ceremony
journey.quote: Families settle the list between themselves, and it varies widely.
journey.reaction: Fair enough, and I'd rather that than a made-up figure. But as the bride's mother, am I meant to be writing this list? I'd want someone to quietly tell me how it's done so I don't put my foot in it.

journey.quote: At many Yoruba engagements, the groom and his friends lie prostrate before the bride's parents and elders when they arrive.
journey.reaction: Goodness. I'd like to know that before it happens rather than stand there looking startled. Glad it's explained.

journey.quote: It is worn by both men and women, it is typically striped, and certain pieces are reserved for special religious, communal or family occasions.
journey.reaction: Interesting, but this cloth history is more than I need. I skimmed to find out what I'd actually wear.

journey.section: 8. Igba nkwu, the wine carrying ceremony
journey.quote: She sips the wine and walks through the guests in search of the groom, then offers him the cup. He drinks, and together they return it to her father.
journey.reaction: That's lovely. Her father is part of it. I'm sending this bit to my husband so he's not caught out.

journey.quote: Guests usually buy their own fabric from the family and arrange their own tailoring.
journey.reaction: So our side buys fabric from the groom's family? Or does the bride's family sell it to ours? Who's handling the money there? I'd want that very clear before the aunties start ringing me.

journey.section: 10. Spraying money: why Nigerians throw money at weddings
journey.quote: The couple are usually sprayed together, and parents and close family take their turn on the floor.
journey.reaction: Parents dance up too. I'd need to know roughly how much cash to bring and in what notes. It doesn't say, and I'd rather ask quietly than look mean on the dance floor.

journey.section: Travel to Nigeria for family: what Smartraveller says
journey.quote: Many families choose instead to hold every ceremony in Australia, or at a destination where relatives from Nigeria, the United Kingdom and North America can meet.
journey.reaction: Sensible. But if it's at another destination, nothing here talks about older guests: transfers, accessibility, medical care, travel insurance. My mother uses a walking frame. That's what I'd need to know.

journey.section: Timing the traditional and white weddings
journey.quote: Many diaspora couples hold the traditional wedding and the white wedding or nikah on consecutive days, so relatives who travel need only make one trip.
journey.reaction: Yes. One trip, please. That's the sort of practical point I appreciate.

journey.section: Timing the traditional and white weddings
journey.quote: If any part of the marriage takes place overseas, ask a lawyer and your celebrant how it will be recognised.
journey.reaction: Good, honest. Tells me who to ask rather than pretending.

journey.section: Music, the alaga or MC and room for spraying
journey.quote: Who will gather the notes during spraying, and where will they be kept safe?
journey.reaction: Exactly my kind of question. Someone has thought about the money being looked after.

journey.section: Music, the alaga or MC and room for spraying
journey.quote: They work in your time zone and quote in AUD, the fee is agreed in writing before any work begins, and your advisor confirms the inclusions in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: That's the sentence I was hunting for. Australian dollars, in writing, before anything starts. It still doesn't say what happens to deposits paid to venues, or who I ring if something goes wrong on the day.

journey.section: Music, the alaga or MC and room for spraying
journey.quote: The nikah, the church service, any legal steps and every family custom stay with you, your families, your celebrant and your faith leaders.
journey.reaction: Clear about who's responsible for what. I respect that.

journey.quote: It depends on the family. The groom and his family bring the bride price and the list, and the costs of the celebration are shared in many different ways.
journey.reaction: That's the question I came for, and the answer is a bit of a shrug. I understand it varies, but I'd like even one line on what the bride's side usually covers, or who can help us have that conversation.

journey.section: Planning your Nigerian wedding with us
journey.quote: You will meet one Wedded Advisor, your single point of contact from the first call to the wedding day.
journey.reaction: One person and a first call. That's what I want. I'd still like to know it's a phone call I can have before anything is booked.

unanswered_questions: As the bride's family, what are we usually expected to contribute, and can someone help both families agree it without awkwardness?
If we pay deposits to venues or suppliers, especially at an overseas destination, is that money protected, and what happens if plans change?
Who do I ring if something goes wrong on the day? Is anyone from your side there?
If the wedding is at another destination, can an elderly guest with a walking frame manage transfers and venues, and what travel insurance and medical cover should she have?
How much cash should parents bring for spraying, and in what notes?
With aso ebi, who sells the fabric to our side and who collects the money?
What should a non-Nigerian mother of the bride wear, and is it fine to ask?
Who is the Wedded Advisor, and can I speak with them on the phone before anything is booked?
would_share_with: My husband, with the wine carrying ceremony, the Smartraveller line and the 'who pays' answer marked
My daughter, to ask what our side is expected to bring to the list and whether Nana can manage two weddings

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready to talk through dates, places or a wedding at home, tell us your date, your guest list and the feeling you want. Nothing is too early or too vague.
cta_reaction.why: 'Nothing is too early or too vague' is kind, and I'd feel I could ask my practical questions without looking old-fashioned. The fee in writing and one named contact help. But there's no button or phone number right there at the end, and I want to know a real person will ring me before anything is booked.

top_3_changes: In the 'Who pays' FAQ or the timing section, add a line for the bride's family on how to start the cost conversation between both families (written as questions to ask, not invented figures), since parents funding the day will look for it.
In the travel section, add a short note for older or less mobile guests at a destination wedding (transfers, accessibility, medical cover, travel insurance), framed as questions to ask.

At the closing invitation, give a visible link or next step and say plainly that it starts with a phone call with a named person, plus how deposits and on-the-day support are handled, or list them as questions to ask.

checks.check: Every journey point, turn-off and CTA reaction has an exact quote from the draft
Stayed in character as Margaret (funding parent, practical, reads top to bottom)
No invented brand facts; missing business details listed as unanswered questions
HTML comments, image slots and VERIFY markers treated as invisible
Title and deferred business details not raised as must-fix, per orchestrator

open_questions.question: Deposit protection, on-the-day support and accessibility for elderly guests remain this persona's main trust gaps, but business details are deferred. Treat as nice-to-have or route to CRO for the CTA block?
The closing section has no visible link (the primary CTA is only a marker). Should the closing invitation carry a link and say a phone call is the next step?

assumptions: Margaret reads the whole article on an iPad because her daughter sent it.
Persona card gives no Nigerian heritage; reactions assume she is the non-Nigerian bride's mother and the groom's family is Nigerian.
Per orchestrator, brand voice does not discuss sourcing; the cloth-history comment is a readability point, not a request for sourcing commentary.
